title: Tourism hackathon to seek solutions for industry challenges
content:
The Department of Tourism, together with the University of Cape Town (UCT), will launch the Tourism Hackathon Challenge in Cape Town this weekend.

“[The] Minister of Tourism Patricia de Lille will officially launch the initiative that will bring together young innovators to develop practical, technology-driven solutions for challenges facing the tourism sector. The Tourism hackathon is a collaborative event in which young innovators work in teams to develop practical, technology-driven solutions for the tourism sector,” the Department of Tourism said in a statement on Thursday.

Set to get underway at the University of Cape Town (UCT DSchool) on Saturday, the hackathon will culminate in the presentation of working prototypes that aim to strengthen and improve the visibility of township and rural operators, whilst providing online solutions that connect them to new markets.

“Investing in the sustainability of the tourism sector begins with an investment in the youth. Through the hackathon, we want to build a pipeline of young talent who will not only gain digital skills, mentorship and practical experience, but who will be encouraged to pursue careers and entrepreneurship through innovation in tourism,” the Minister said.

Building on the success of the inaugural 2025 G20 Tourism Hackathon, this year’s challenge is themed: “Community-Based Tourism and Rural Inclusion”.

Fifty students, selected from public and private universities offering tourism and hospitality qualifications, will work in teams to develop solutions in the following areas:
- Digital platforms that connect tourists with township and rural experiences,
- Online booking systems for local guides, homestays, and village experiences,
- Virtual-reality tours that highlight hidden gems, and
- Payment and financial inclusion solutions for small tourism operators.

The department has partnered with UCT and various multi-sector stakeholders, including the Culture, Arts, Tourism, Hospitality and Sport Sector Education and Training Authority (CATHSSETA), the Centre for Public Service Innovation (CPSI), Future Leaders Challenge and Geekculture, to implement the hackathon.

“We are pleased to have partnered with UCT on our quest to propel innovation in the tourism sector. This hackathon is a key aspect of the Tourism Growth Partnership Plan (TGPP) 2025–2030 to drive tourism product development, job creation, skills development, and economic empowerment through community inclusion.”

“Tourism is open to innovation that will enhance travel experiences, whilst laying the foundation for entrepreneurial opportunities for the youth,” the Minister explained.

She further added that the department’s collaboration with UCT will draw on the institution's expertise in design thinking, innovation, entrepreneurship and financial technology to strengthen the development of practical solutions for the tourism sector.

Beyond the competition, the Department of Tourism and UCT will explore opportunities to support the top three finalists through relevant innovation and entrepreneurship development programmes.

Teams will refine their concepts after the launch, ahead of the final pitching and awards event planned for the fourth quarter of the 2026/27 financial year (January to March 2027).

UCT Vice-Chancellor, Professor Mosa Moshabela said the university said the collaboration reflects a shared commitment to strengthening tourism through innovation.

"The University of Cape Town is proud to enter into this three-year strategic partnership with the Department of Tourism. This collaboration reflects our shared commitment to strengthening tourism through innovation, entrepreneurship and the creation of new opportunities across the sector.  "It also aligns with UCT’s Strategy 2030 and our commitment to advancing impactful partnerships that drive sustainable development,” Moshabela said.

The Tourism Hackathon strategically contributes to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), which promotes sustainable tourism that creates jobs and promotes local culture and products, and SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure). Through its multi-stakeholder collaboration, it also advances SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals). -SAnews.gov.za

title: Cachalia condemns the killing of Station Commander in KZN
content: The Acting Minister of Police, Firoz Cachalia, has strongly condemned the killing of a Station Commander who was shot while responding to a business robbery in Greytown, KwaZulu-Natal. The South African Police Service (SAPS) Lieutenant Colonel was shot on Thursday. The Acting Minister has described the killing as a senseless and cowardly attack on a police officer who was carrying out her constitutional responsibility to protect communities and uphold the law. “The Station Commander demonstrated exceptional courage and commitment to duty by personally leading her members in responding to the robbery, during which a business owner was shot and injured, and employees were assaulted,” the Minister said.  A Sergeant was also shot and injured during the exchange of gunfire and is receiving medical attention.  The Acting Minister commends the police members who responded to the robbery and pursued the suspects, as well as the collaboration between SAPS and private security during the operation.  Cachalia extended his deepest condolences to the family, friends and colleagues of the fallen Station Commander and also wishes the injured police officer a speedy recovery. – SAnews.gov.za

title: Chikunga welcomes R5.1bn boost to strengthen government’s GBVF response
IEC gazettes names of councillors elected in 2026 local government polls
content:
The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has gazetted the names of councillors elected in the 2026 Local Government Elections -- a step that triggers preparations for the first sittings of municipal councils. Addressing the media in Pretoria on Friday, IEC Chairperson Mosotho Moepya, said municipal managers must convene the first meeting of their councils within 14 days after councillors are declared elected. “The publication of the list of councillors today, 13 November 2026, will enable planning for the inaugural sittings of the municipal councils,” Moepya said. The Commission said the publication follows the announcement of election results on Sunday, 8 November, and the completion of processes required before elected councillors’ names could be gazetted. These included notifying parties that had nominated fewer proportional representation (PR) candidates than the number of seats they won, and asking parties or independent candidates to choose between multiple seats to which they are entitled. Parties had until Wednesday, 11 November, to make up candidate-list shortfalls or indicate which seat a candidate would take.  The Commission said this was not an opportunity to change candidate lists or replace nominees.  A party that failed to provide enough names could forfeit seats if the shortfall made it impossible for a municipal council to form a quorum. Five ward by-elections will be scheduled after the elections. Two are now required after parties redesignated councillors who won more than one ward seat -- Ward 12 in Johannes Phumani Pungula Municipality in KwaZulu-Natal and Ward 13 in Dihlabeng Municipality in the Free State. Three further by-elections follow the deaths of ward councillors -- Ward 16 in Raymond Mhlaba Municipality in the Eastern Cape, Ward 12 in Merafong Municipality in Gauteng and Ward 17 in uMlalazi Municipality in KwaZulu-Natal. Four ward contests were decided by lot after candidates received an equal number of votes. The winning parties were the African National Congress in Ward 7 of Mnquma Municipality in the Eastern Cape and Ward 5 of Ba-Phalaborwa Municipality in Limpopo; the African Content Movement in Ward 14 of Maluti-a-Phofung Municipality in the Free State, and the South African Communist Party in Ward 17 of Steve Tshwete Municipality in Mpumalanga. There are 10 526 seats available across the 2026 elections. These comprise 8 825 local council seats, 4 485 ward seats and 4 340 PR seats, and 1 701 district council seats. Of the district seats, 707 are directly elected and 994 will be filled by representatives elected from local councils. Women make up 33.6% of declared councillors, including 39.7% of PR councillors and 26.8% of ward councillors. The average age of councillors is 47.3 years. Councillors under 35 account for 10.8% of the total. The Commission also provided an update on objections under section 65 of the Municipal Structures Act. 

By noon on Friday, it had received 1 708 submissions, of which 433 were deemed to be section 65 objections. Of those, 252 had been finalised, three were upheld and 249 rejected. The decisions involved 12 recounts and seven edit windows, in addition to a revote in the Northern Cape scheduled for next week. The Commission said the gazetted list excludes councillors for Siyancuma Municipality in the Northern Cape. The seat calculation and assignment there will be completed after a revote in a voting district in Ward 3. Special voting is scheduled for 17 November and voting for 18 November. Moepya said the published list has several consequences, including establishing the effective date of councillors’ election and enabling district council preparations. “The first is that the representatives are deemed to have been elected as councillors with effect from 8 November 2026 (the date of the result announcement),” Moepya said. The Commission also reported a judgment in the Ngcobo Municipality impersonation matter. The Electoral Court barred the candidate who impersonated an IEC staff member from holding councillor office for the five-year term of councils elected on 4 November. The candidate’s accomplice was fined R100 000, suspended for three years. – SAnews.gov.za

title: Government acknowledges gaps in justice system's GBVF response
content: Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities, Sindisiwe Chikunga, has acknowledged persistent shortcomings in the criminal justice system's response to gender-based violence and femicide (GBVF), despite progress in strengthening institutional capacity and survivor support services. Chikunga said challenges relating to access to justice, secondary victimisation, case management, investigative capacity, conviction rates, and coordination continue to undermine the experiences of survivors within the criminal justice system.  The Minister was speaking during a strategic engagement with the Commission for Gender Equality (CGE) on Friday, 13 November 2026, focusing on the implementation of Pillar 3 of the National Strategic Plan on GBVF (NSP-GBVF), which deals with Justice, Safety and Protection. The engagement follows a CGE study examining implementation challenges under the pillar, including the reporting, victim support, investigation, prosecution and sentencing of GBVF cases. Chikunga welcomed the Commission's oversight work, including its joint inquiry with the South African Human Rights Commission and the CRL Rights Commission, which included engagements in Mpumalanga, the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal.  She said the findings provided government with important evidence on the challenges experienced by survivors and the institutions responsible for supporting them.  “These challenges are real, and government remains committed to addressing them decisively,” Chikunga said.  Providing an update on implementation, Chikunga noted that Pillar 3 recorded the strongest five-year performance among the six pillars of the NSP-GBVF. Of the 54 indicators under the pillar, 31 have been achieved, while 14 are in progress, with nine not being achieved.  She said progress included the upgrading of 40 district courts to improve support for survivors of domestic violence, while 14 sexual offences courts were established in the financial year ending March 2026. A total of 338 functional testimony facilities are also available to support remote or protected testimony. In addition, 153 847 National Register for Sex Offenders clearance certificates have been issued over the past five years, with 79 179 issued by March 2026. The Minister said the National Prosecuting Authority has also strengthened its response through specialised training, with 221 prosecutors having completed GBVF training against a target of 800. Between January and June 2026, a further 1 185 law enforcement officers participated in GBV-related learning programmes aimed at improving investigations, prosecutions, and victim support services. However, Chikunga warned that improvements in institutional capacity have not yet translated into consistently timely and survivor-centred outcomes. She pointed to the worsening backlog of sexual offences cases and uneven evidence on how cases progress through the criminal justice system, the quality of services and survivors' experiences. “Although system capacity has improved, timely, survivor-centred case outcomes remain the real test,” she said. Strengthening reporting and accountability The Minister said the Department of Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities, as custodian of the NSP-GBVF, is strengthening monitoring, reporting, and accountability across government to improve implementation. She highlighted that the department has established more than 40 Rapid Response Teams in districts and municipalities to improve coordination in responding to GBVF incidents. The department has also deployed European Union-funded technical monitors and data collectors across provincial Offices of the Premiers to strengthen reporting and evidence-based planning. Through the 100-Day Challenges initiative, implementation has expanded across all nine provinces, with between 46 and 50 municipalities participating. A national GBVF services dashboard has also been developed to map available services and support better planning and resource allocation. Chikunga said the next phase of implementation will prioritise survivor-centred justice services, improved coordination across the criminal justice value chain, stronger data systems, and accountability across government departments. The Minister reaffirmed government's commitment to working with the CGE and other stakeholders to address the identified gaps and improve services for survivors. She reiterated that ending GBVF requires sustained collaboration between government, civil society, communities, and all sectors of society. – SAnews.gov.za

title: Hlabisa pushes for operational SADC disaster centre
content: Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (CoGTA) Minister Velenkosini Hlabisa has called for the full operationalisation of the SADC Humanitarian and Emergency Operations Centre (SHOC) to strengthen the region's capacity to coordinate disaster preparedness and respond swiftly to emergencies.  Hlabisa, who chairs the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Committee of Ministers Responsible for Disaster Risk Management, said the centre should serve as a regional anchor for disaster monitoring, early warning, preparedness coordination and the mobilisation of assistance to Member States affected by disasters. Addressing the 7th Ordinary Meeting of the Committee on Thursday, 12 November 2026, the Minister said effective regional coordination requires clear authority, capable leadership, adequate staffing, reliable operating procedures, and sustainable financing. He called for the recruitment of SHOC's Executive Director to be concluded in accordance with the approved roadmap, while urging State Parties to fulfil their assessed contribution obligations. He also encouraged Member States that have not yet joined the centre to accede, emphasising the importance of collective commitment to strengthening regional disaster response mechanisms. Hlabisa said the first SADC Regional Cyclone and Flood Response Simulation Exercise has demonstrated the value of testing regional systems before disasters strike.  He called for such exercises to become a regular feature of regional preparedness efforts to identify and address weaknesses in decision-making, early warning, authorisation, deployment and coordination. He said the exercises will help ensure that regional institutions and Member States are better prepared to respond when emergencies occur.  “Disaster risk does not respect national borders, and no Member State should be left to confront a major disaster alone. Regional solidarity must be organised in advance, adequately resourced and capable of being activated when it is most needed,” the Minister said. The meeting also considered regional climate risks, food and nutrition security, disaster preparedness, humanitarian logistics and anticipatory action.  Hlabisa urged Ministers to ensure that the outcomes of their deliberations translate into concrete decisions and implementation, stressing the need to turn regional knowledge into national action and strengthen collective resilience across Southern Africa. – SAnews.gov.za

title: SADC countries urged to strengthen disaster readiness
content:
Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (CoGTA) Minister Velenkosini Hlabisa has called on Southern African Development Community (SADC) Member States to urgently strengthen disaster preparedness and secure funding ahead of the 2026/27 rainfall season.

Speaking at the virtual 7th SADC Committee of Ministers Meeting Responsible for Disaster Risk Management on Thursday, Hlabisa said the state of preparedness for the coming season demands equally serious attention, warning that a regional snapshot indicates that around 41 million people may be at risk.

In his address, Hlabisa, who chaired the meeting, said preparedness and response requirements are estimated at US $1.85 billion, against about $241 million currently available. The Minister said the severe financing gap requires Member States to move beyond "expressions of concern".

“Contingency plans that are not approved, financed, tested and understood by those responsible for implementation cannot protect communities.

“This severe financing gap requires us to move beyond expressions of concern and towards costed plans, assigned responsibilities, pre-arranged financing and measurable implementation,” he said.

The Minister urged Member States to finalise and validate El Niño-informed contingency plans, identify triggers and early actions, secure resources, pre-position essential supplies and strengthen coordination across sectors and across borders.

The Minister said the outlook for the 2026/27 rainfall season requires urgent and differentiated interventions, with strong El Niño conditions, elevated temperatures and below-normal rainfall expected across much of central and southern SADC. Northern, coastal and island areas, however, may remain exposed to flooding and other high-rainfall hazards.

He said the region must prepare for multiple threats, including drought, heat stress, water shortages, floods, severe storms, wildfires and disease outbreaks, and cascading impacts on agriculture, energy, health, infrastructure, and regional markets.

“Preparedness cannot be uniform when risk is not uniform. Regional assessments must be translated into downscaled national and subnational forecasts, practical advisories and early decisions that reach institutions, farmers, and communities in time to act,” the Minister said.

Hlabisa said the improved agricultural production, pasture conditions, water availability, and regional food supply recorded during the 2025/26 rainfall season must not create a false sense of security.

Although the season supported a broad recovery, floods, tropical cyclones, localised dry spells and disease outbreaks continued to cause loss of life, displacement, infrastructure damage and livelihood disruptions.

“The message is clear: an improved regional outlook does not mean that vulnerability has been overcome. It means that we have a narrow opportunity to protect recent gains before the next shock reverses them.”

The Minister also raised concerns about food insecurity, noting that approximately 53 million people in reporting Member States are projected to face food insecurity during the 2026/27 consumption period.

He noted that food insecurity is driven not only by agricultural production, but also by poverty, conflict, displacement, rising food prices, limited market access, household income and the affordability of nutritious food.

He called for a comprehensive response combining resilient agriculture, functioning regional trade, nutrition interventions, livelihood protection and social protection measures that could respond to climate-related shocks.

The Minister emphasised that early-warning systems must translate into practical interventions before communities experience the full impact of disasters.

He also highlighted the SADC Multi-Hazard Regional Anticipatory Action Framework 2026–2030 as an important mechanism for linking weather forecasts and agreed triggers to pre-arranged interventions.

He said measures to protect agricultural planting, water access, livestock, household income and essential services need to be activated before the impacts of climate hazards become fully visible.

“Early warning is valuable only when it leads to early decisions, early financing and early action,” Hlabisa said.

The Minister also highlighted the importance of strengthening regional humanitarian logistics through the SADC Regional Prepositioning Strategy, which aims to improve the availability, location and movement of emergency relief supplies.

He said administrative and logistical delays should not prevent humanitarian assistance from reaching communities when disasters strike, calling for clear procedures, interoperable systems and efficient cross-border support arrangements. – SAnews.gov.za

title: Two arrested for unlawfully issuing driver’s licence
content: Two suspects have been arrested for allegedly manipulating the electronic National Traffic Information System (eNaTIS) to fraudulently issue a Traffic Register Number (TRN) and a driver’s licence. The Road Traffic Management Corporation (RTMC), working with the South African Police Service (SAPS) Anti-Corruption Unit, arrested a traffic officer and a clerk stationed at the Adelaide Driving Licence Testing Centre (DLTC) on Wednesday. The two are accused of colluding to unlawfully issue the documents. One of the suspects allegedly received cash deposits from an applicant seeking assistance to obtain a TRN and a driver’s licence on 23 January 2024. The RTMC said investigations established that the clerk had allegedly issued a TRN to the applicant in her absence. “It was further established that the TRN had initially been allocated to another male individual but was subsequently altered on the eNaTIS system. “Investigators also uncovered communication between the applicant and the traffic officer, as well as several payments of varying amounts made directly into his bank account. These payments were allegedly made in exchange for facilitating the applicant’s acquisition of the TRN,” the RTMC said in a statement on Friday. The applicant maintained that she had never visited the Adelaide DLTC to apply for or obtain the TRN. However, eNaTIS records indicated that the TRN had been issued. The suspects are expected to make their first appearance before the Specialised Commercial Crimes Court on 10 December 2026, where they will face charges of corruption and fraud. The RTMC said it remains committed to working with law enforcement agencies to root out corruption within the road traffic environment, strengthen accountability and protect the integrity of the country’s road traffic administration systems. - SAnews.gov.za

title: eThekwini focuses on infrastructure to sustain employment growth
content: eThekwini City Manager Musa Mbhele has emphasised the need to strengthen municipal infrastructure, improve service delivery and create an enabling environment for investment to sustain the city's positive employment growth. Mbhele’s remarks follow the release of Statistics South Africa's Quarterly Labour Force Survey for the third quarter of 2026, which shows that eThekwini was the only metropolitan municipality in the country to record a decline in its unemployment rate over the year. The survey, covering the period July to September 2026, shows that the city's official unemployment rate dropped from 27.8% in the third quarter of 2025 to 22.2% in the corresponding period this year, representing a decrease of 5.6 percentage points. This places eThekwini level with the City of Cape Town as the metropolitan municipalities with the lowest unemployment rate in the country, and significantly below the national rate of 33.7%. Commenting on the figures, Mbhele said the improved employment performance is encouraging, but the municipality remained focused on the structural interventions needed to sustain long-term economic growth. “These figures reflect an encouraging expansion in employment, indicating that more of our residents are engaged in productive work compared to a year ago – a welcome development for households across the municipality. It is particularly noteworthy that eThekwini has bucked the broader national trend during a period of rising unemployment in other regions,” Mbhele said. Between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, the number of unemployed residents in eThekwini decreased by 101 000, from 464 000 to 363 000. Over the same period, the number of employed residents increased by 66 000 to 1.27 million, the largest employment gain recorded by any metropolitan municipality. Formal sector employment in the city also increased by 146 000, representing growth of 18.2%. Mbhele said the municipality's economic mandate is to establish a predictable and enabling environment that builds investor confidence and supports enterprise development. “Our primary responsibility as an administration is execution excellence: securing robust infrastructure for water and electricity, maintaining clean and safe public amenities, and streamlining regulatory processes to facilitate investment in Durban. “Our strategic focus remains firmly fixed on these fundamentals, driven by collaborative partnerships with business, organised labour and all spheres of government,” he said. The full Quarterly Labour Force Survey, Quarter 3: 2026, is available on the Statistics South Africa website at www.statssa.gov.za – SAnews.gov.za

title: Nelson Mandela Bay prepares for safe summer initiation season
content: Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality has stepped up preparations for the upcoming summer initiation season following refresher training for traditional surgeons and assistants, with a renewed focus on health, safety and legal compliance. The training was organised by the Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality Initiation Forum, in collaboration with the Department of Health, and was held at three venues across the metro between 7 and 9 November 2026. The sessions took place at the LoveLife Centre in Kariega on 7 November, Raymond Mhlaba Sport Complex in Motherwell on 8 November and Mendi Arts Centre in New Brighton on 9 November.  The training aimed to strengthen the readiness of traditional surgeons and assistants (Iingcibi namaKhankatha), while updating practitioners and other stakeholders on the latest health, safety and legal requirements governing the initiation process. The municipality has urged prospective initiates, parents and guardians to ensure that all medical screenings, consent procedures and other compliance requirements are completed before the initiation process begins. Parents and guardians are required to obtain and complete the prescribed forms issued by the Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (CoGTA). They are available through ward councillor offices. The municipality said 5 500 forms have already been distributed in Nelson Mandela Bay, resulting in stocks being depleted. A second batch is expected to be available at ward councillor offices by 23 November 2026. Prospective initiates are also required to undergo an initial medical examination at least three months before their intended circumcision date. According to the municipality, no prescribed form is required for this initial medical assessment, which is intended to identify any underlying health conditions that may require treatment before the initiate participates in the customary practice. “Where a medical condition is identified, the prospective initiate must receive appropriate treatment, followed by a second medical examination 14 days before undergoing the traditional initiation process in order to confirm that the initiate is medically fit to participate,” the municipality explained. The municipality has also urged parents and guardians to help prospective initiates maintain good health ahead of the initiation period. This includes ensuring that they eat a balanced diet, drink sufficient water, abstain from sexual intercourse and alcohol consumption, avoid attending imiguyo (pre-initiation send-off gatherings), maintain a positive state of mind, and avoid unnecessary stress associated with the rite of passage. Parents and guardians are encouraged to monitor their children's conduct and be alert to sudden changes in their behaviour or health, seeking medical assistance where necessary. The municipality has further reminded parents, guardians, traditional surgeons, assistants and other stakeholders that customary male initiation must be conducted in accordance with the applicable legislative framework. The national framework is governed by the Customary Initiation Act, 2021 (Act No. 2 of 2021), which regulates customary initiation practices and initiation schools, while outlining the responsibilities of parents, traditional leaders, traditional surgeons, caregivers and government structures. The Act also provides for the registration of initiation schools and establishes national and provincial oversight structures. The framework is further supported by the Customary Initiation Regulations, 2025, which set out requirements for monitoring, inspections, investigations and enforcement of compliance. In the Eastern Cape, customary male initiation is also regulated by the Eastern Cape Customary Male Initiation Practice Act, 2016 (Act No. 5 of 2016), and its accompanying regulations. These provide for provincial coordination structures and outline the responsibilities of parents, traditional leaders, traditional surgeons and traditional nurses, as well as requirements relating to permission, initiation schools and the protection of initiates. The national legislation also recognises provincial-specific provisions and establishes that the national Act takes precedence where there is a conflict with applicable provincial legislation. “The municipality calls on all role-players to work together to ensure that the upcoming summer initiation season is conducted in a safe, lawful, dignified and culturally respectful manner, with the protection of the lives, health and wellbeing of all initiates remaining the priority. “The municipality further urges parents and guardians to ensure that their children only attend properly registered initiation schools and that all required medical, consent and legal processes are completed before the initiation process begins.” – SAnews.gov.za

title: eThekwini welcomes commercial development investment
content:
The eThekwini Municipality has welcomed a R250 million investment in a new commercial office development at Sibaya Coastal City, describing it as a boost to the city's economic growth, job creation and municipal revenue.

Devmco Group, the master developer of the Sibaya region, officially launched HQ Sibaya, a 7 000-square-metre premium office development, on Tuesday.

Located along Heleza Boulevard, between uMhlanga, uMdloti and King Shaka International Airport, the development forms part of efforts to establish Sibaya as an integrated mixed-use urban node, bringing together residential, commercial, retail and lifestyle facilities.

According to the developer, the project is expected to generate approximately R500 million in total economic output, based on National Treasury's economic multiplier. It is also projected to contribute an estimated R8 million annually to the municipality's rates base.

The development is expected to create approximately 750 temporary jobs during construction, with a further 20 permanent positions once operational.

The Devmco Group said 75% of the available office space has already been sold, with full occupancy anticipated within the first year of completion.

City Manager Musa Mbhele said the development demonstrates the municipality's commitment to facilitating investment-led growth and expanding sustainable economic opportunities.

“HQ Sibaya represents far more than a new office development. It is an investment in the future of our city and a catalyst for economic growth. Projects of this nature attract business, create employment, expand the municipal rates base, and strengthen the competitiveness of our regional economy.

“Through strategic partnerships with the private sector, we are building vibrant, mixed-use urban environments that support investment, innovation and long-term prosperity,” Mbhele said.

Devmco Group Managing Director Schalk Theunissen said the project marks an important milestone in the development of Sibaya as a fully integrated coastal city.

“HQ Sibaya marks the start of the commercial node and creates further opportunities for people to work and live within one coastal city. As Sibaya continues to develop, each new component strengthens the wider vision of creating an integrated environment where residential, commercial, retail and lifestyle uses work together,” Theunissen said.

Construction of the building's upper structure is expected to begin once earthworks have been completed, with the development scheduled for completion in the fourth quarter of 2027.

The municipality has reaffirmed its commitment to working with private-sector partners to attract investment, stimulate economic activity and support job creation as part of its vision to become Africa's most caring and liveable city by 2030. – SAnews.gov.za

title: Letsike calls for inclusive access to sport
content: Deputy Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities Mmapaseka Letsike has called for greater inclusion in sport, saying children should be free to pursue the games they love without being made to feel they do not belong. Addressing a men’s netball tournament on Thursday, Letsike reflected on her own experience as a football-loving girl, who helped establish the first girls’ football team at her high school. She said the name "Steve" had stayed with her since those days on the football field. “So here I am, a woman called Steve because she played football, addressing men who play netball. The irony is delightful. But beneath it lies a question that matters deeply to me: how many gifted children are made to feel that the game they love was not meant for them?” Letsike said exclusion can begin through everyday attitudes, including jokes and dismissive comments that discourage children from taking part. “That kind of exclusion rarely begins with a written rule. It begins with a joke, a dismissive look, an adult who tells a child to choose a different game. We may call it harmless teasing, but a child can carry those words for years. The cost is not only wounded confidence; it is talent our country never gets to discover,” Letsike said. Letsike said the tournament represents more than competition, as the athletes’ participation could help widen opportunities for others. “Yet by taking your place on this court, you also widen the horizon for the boy who loves netball, just as generations of women widened it for girls who love football,” she said. Letsike said government has a responsibility to turn the constitutional promises of dignity, freedom and substantive equality into everyday opportunities.  She added that inclusion requires accessible facilities, community-based opportunities and public institutions that consider who might still be excluded. “This means asking difficult questions. Can a child in a township find a safe court and a coach? Can a young person in a rural community afford to travel to a tournament? Can an athlete with a disability participate on equal terms? During Disability Rights Awareness Month, we must recognise that inclusion is not a favour; it is a public responsibility,” Letsike said. She stressed that the growth of men’s netball should be matched by greater investment in women’s sport. “The growth of men’s netball must go hand in hand with greater investment in women’s sport. Equality is not achieved by moving exclusion from one group to another; it is achieved when the doors are opened wider for everyone,” she said. With International Men’s Day approaching and the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence and Femicide ahead, Letsike urged men to carry the values of sport into their communities. “Real strength is not control over another person. It is the confidence to respect difference, the discipline to reject violence, and the courage to stand against prejudice, including the growing anti-gender backlash,” she said. Letsike called on Netball South Africa, municipalities, schools, sporting bodies and sponsors to support accessible facilities, community leagues, trained coaches and development pathways. “Let us measure success not only in trophies, but in the young people who are able to enter the game because we acted together,” she said. Welcoming participants from across Southern Africa, Letsike said sport could strengthen friendship and solidarity across borders. She encouraged athletes to compete passionately and honour their opponents. “Football gave me the name Steve. What I hope we give the next generation is something more enduring: the freedom to pursue their gifts without first having to prove that they belong,” Letsike said. – SAnews.gov.za
